props.title: When Dinosaurs Ruled the Earth
props.initialSlug: Cavemen battle dinosaurs in a prehistoric epic

sections.content: The Hammer Films production When Dinosaurs Ruled the Earth represents a fascinating chapter in practical effects dinosaur movies, bridging the gap between the stop-motion mastery of One Million Years B.C. (1966) and modern CGI spectacles. Jim Danforth's Oscar-nominated special effects brought prehistoric creatures to life through meticulous animation, while Victoria Vetri's Cave-woman Sanna anchored the fantastical narrative. The film follows Hammer's successful formula of combining prehistoric adventure with scantily-clad protagonists, a template established in their earlier The Lost World (1960).

movies.title: The Valley of Gwangi
movies.slug: Cowboys meet dinosaurs in Ray Harryhausen's western-monster mashup

sections.content: The late 1960s marked a golden age for practical effects dinosaur films, with Ray Harryhausen's work on The Valley of Gwangi (1969) setting new standards for stop-motion animation. These films influenced later works like Baby: Secret of the Lost Legend (1985) and even echoed in early CGI attempts like Carnosaur (1993). The practical effects era created a tangible feeling that modern CGI sometimes struggles to replicate, as seen in the contrast between these classics and films like Jurassic World (2015).

What sets When Dinosaurs Ruled the Earth apart is its commitment to creating a prehistoric world without dialogue, using a made-up caveman language. This approach was later echoed in films like Quest for Fire (1981), showing how primitive communication could drive narrative. The film's attention to creating believable dinosaur behavior, despite scientific inaccuracies, influenced later works like The Land Before Time (1988). sections.content: The practical effects techniques used in When Dinosaurs Ruled the Earth represent a crucial evolutionary step between Willis O'Brien's groundbreaking work in King Kong (1933) and the modern era. The film's combination of stop-motion and full-scale props created a template that influenced everything from The Land That Time Forgot (1974) to Dragonslayer (1981), showing how practical effects could create convincing prehistoric creatures before the digital age.
